Part B · Chapter 8

Debugging neural networks

A routine, a lab of broken runs and the tools that find or limit a fault

A network that trains badly shows a loss, and the loss alone rarely shows why. This chapter gives a routine of checks with expected results and a lab of six broken runs on made-up catch records. Other tools help find or limit a fault: gradient norms, the update-to-weight ratio, gradient clipping, a learning-rate range test, learning curves, runs with several seeds, and tests of one component at a time.

You will need: vanishing and exploding slopes (B4), learning rates and Adam (B5), initialisation and normalisation (B6), validation sets and overfitting (A4) and the confidence interval (0.7).

The routine and the starting loss

Guess first. A network will sort sharks into five species. Before any training step, with small random weights, you compute its loss on one batch of sharks. About what should the loss be: 0, 0.5, 1.6 or 5?

When a network trains badly, the loss is the first number we look at, and it rarely shows what is wrong. The routine in the figure lists seven checks in a fixed order, from cheap and general (look at the data) to costly and specific (tune). These checks come with results you can state before you look. One of them is the starting loss, the loss on the first batch before any training step. The loss on one shark is \(-\ln p\), where \(p\) is the probability that the network gives to the shark's true species and \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. With small random weights the network gives the five species almost equal probabilities, so the starting loss can be worked out in advance.

  1. Press Step 1 to Step 7 in turn: the panel says what you do, what the check catches and what result you should see.
  2. Press Step 3, "Check the starting loss": the result to expect for five species is about \(\ln 5 = 1.61\).

The seven checks come with expected results; for the starting loss with five species the result is \(\ln 5 = 1.61\), which answers the guess: about 1.6.

How it works

Suppose the network's five output scores, one per species, are all equal. The softmax (the rule from the probability chapter that turns scores into probabilities) gives equal scores equal probabilities, so \(p = 1/5\) for any species. Then the loss of a shark is \(-\ln(1/5) = \ln 5 = 1.609\) (because \(\ln(1/x) = -\ln x\)), and so is the average over the batch. Small random weights give small output scores that differ little. So a healthy network starts close to this value but not on it (1.48 in the lab of the next section, 1.65 in the repaired pipeline of the last section). If the scores differ widely, a shark whose true species gets a probability near 0 has a very large loss.

\(L_0\)starting loss: 1.609=\(-\ln(1/K)\)minus the log of the probability 1/K=\(\ln K\)K = 5 classes
  1. The curve is the first loss when the five output scores are random numbers of typical size \(s\). Drag the slider to 0.1: the loss is 1.61, the dashed line at \(\ln 5\).
  2. Drag the slider to 2: the loss is 2.81. At 5 it is 6.04, so a first loss far above \(\ln 5\) suggests that the output scores start large.

Common belief. If the starting loss equals \(\ln K\), the network and the code are correct.

Why it fails. The check catches a narrow set of faults: a wrong loss function, output scores that start large, and inputs that are not standardised (first loss 9.1 in the next section). Standardised inputs are rescaled to mean 0 and spread 1. The pipeline with four bugs in the last section of this chapter starts at 1.613, against \(\ln 5 = 1.609\).

Better account. A match is one passed check. Run it whenever you change the loss, the output layer or the number of classes, and write the expected value next to the printed one.

Quick quiz

A network with 10 classes starts with a loss of 2.3. What should a network with 1,000 classes show at the start?

\(\ln 1000 = 6.91\). A loss of 2.3 there would mean that the output is already far from equal probabilities.

A five-class network starts with a loss of 2.81. About how large are its output scores, and what does that suggest?

Their typical size is about 2, from the slider. A first loss far above \(\ln 5 = 1.61\) suggests that the output scores start large, so look at the last layer and at the scale of the inputs.

Where the routine comes from

The routine follows Karpathy's "A Recipe for Training Neural Networks" (2019). It asks you to start by inspecting the data, before any network code. Then you build a complete training and evaluation loop with simple baselines, and overfit before you regularise. The routine also follows Ng's Machine Learning Yearning. Its chapter 13 advises building a first system quickly and iterating. Its chapter 14 shows how to read the dev set examples that a system gets wrong. Both the recipe and the Stanford CS231n notes list the two sanity checks, the starting loss and a tiny training set. The update-to-weight ratio of the next sections comes from the CS231n notes.

Terms of the routine

baseline
a simple model whose score the network must beat (the lazy model of A4)
starting loss
the loss on a batch before any step
overfit one batch
train on 16 sharks until the loss is near 0, as a test of the whole training loop
error analysis
reading the cases the model gets wrong, to see what kind of data or change would help

Two more numbers to know before you look

The CS231n notes make the same check for ten classes: \(\ln 10 = 2.30\). A second number is worth knowing for this data. A network whose output is the species shares of the table (45%, 33%, 12%, 9.5% and 0.5%) has a loss equal to the entropy of the labels, \(-\sum p\ln p = 0.36 + 0.37 + 0.25 + 0.22 + 0.03 = 1.23\). A loss that stays at 1.23 means that the network does no better than one that uses only the base rates.

About the starting-loss figure

The curve is simulated with 40,000 draws of five random scores and a random correct class. A first loss far above 1.6 points to large output scores, and two likely causes are a last layer that starts too large and inputs that are not standardised. The code below uses 200,000 draws, so its values differ from the figure's by up to 0.03.

The check in symbols

\[ L_0 \;=\; -\ln\frac{1}{K} \;=\; \ln K \]

  • \(L_0\) is the cross-entropy loss before training. \(K\) is the number of classes, 5 for the species.
  • The formula assumes that the scores are all close to 0, so softmax gives all classes the probability \(1/K\) (0.7). The figure shows what happens when they are not.

Why the loss grows with the score size

Let the five starting scores be random with spread \(s\) around 0. For small \(s\), expand \(\ln\sum_k e^{z_k}\) to second order. It is \(\ln K + \bar z + \tfrac12\,\mathrm{var}(z)\), where \(\bar z\) is the mean of the \(K\) scores of a shark and \(\mathrm{var}(z)\) their variance across the classes. The loss of a shark is this minus the score of its true class. That score has mean 0, and the variance across classes averages \(s^2(1 - 1/K)\). So the loss is about \(\ln K + \tfrac12 s^2(1 - 1/K)\), which is \(1.609 + 0.4\,s^2\) here. For large \(s\) the largest score dominates, and the loss is about the gap between the largest of five random scores and the score of the true class. That gap averages \(1.16\,s\). The simulation is close to the first line up to \(s = 0.5\) and to the second only for large \(s\). At \(s = 0.1\) the first gives 1.613 against a simulated 1.614. At \(s = 5\) the second gives 5.8 against 6.0. At \(s = 2\) the simulation, 2.80, lies between the two formulas (3.21 and 2.32).

In Python

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
K = 5
for s in [0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5]:                                 # spread of the random output scores
    z = rng.normal(0, s, (200000, K)); y = rng.integers(0, K, 200000)
    loss = np.log(np.exp(z).sum(1)) - z[np.arange(200000), y]
    small = np.log(K) + 0.5 * s**2 * (1 - 1 / K)              # formula for small s
    print("s = %.1f  simulated %.3f  small-s formula %5.3f  large-s formula %.2f" % (s, loss.mean(), small, 1.16 * s))

shares = np.array([268, 200, 72, 57, 3]) / 600                # species shares of the 600 made-up records
print("a network that knows only the shares scores %.3f" % -(shares * np.log(shares)).sum())
s = 0.1  simulated 1.614  small-s formula 1.613  large-s formula 0.12
s = 0.5  simulated 1.706  small-s formula 1.709  large-s formula 0.58
s = 1.0  simulated 1.974  small-s formula 2.009  large-s formula 1.16
s = 2.0  simulated 2.804  small-s formula 3.209  large-s formula 2.32
s = 5.0  simulated 6.012  small-s formula 11.609  large-s formula 5.80
a network that knows only the shares scores 1.231

The code also prints the loss of a network whose output is the species shares: 1.231, the entropy of the labels.

The same check for a regression

A network whose outputs are near 0 starts with a mean squared error close to the mean of the squared targets. For the weights of all 600 made-up sharks that is 19.1 kg\(^2\). The code of the clipping section prints 5.70 for 32 ordinary sharks and 346.83 for the 32 heaviest. The mean squared weights of those two groups are 5.3 and 344.7, so the printed losses are close to what an untrained network with outputs near 0 shows.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the starting loss is much lower than \(\ln K\), look for label leakage (a copy of the label among the inputs) or for a mistake in the loss calculation. A network with random weights should not predict the labels well. If it is far above, look at the last layer's size and at the input scale.

More questions

Why try to overfit 16 sharks before training on 480?

On 16 sharks a correct loop can reach a loss near 0, because the network has far more weights than examples. If it cannot, the fault is in the model, the loss or the update step, and it is easier to find on 16 examples than on 480.

The broken-run lab

Guess first. A training run on the made-up catch records ends with the loss at 1.23 and a validation accuracy of 48%, the same as the lazy model, which always says the commonest species. How many different faults can produce that picture: one, two, or three or more?

A symptom is what a run's log shows, and one symptom can have several causes, the faults behind it. To tell the causes apart, the lab records three numbers for the layers. The gradient norm is the length of the loss slopes of a layer's weights. The update-to-weight ratio is the size of a step divided by the size of the weights. The third number is the share of dead units. A dead unit is a ReLU unit (it outputs 0 when its input is negative) that outputs 0 for all training sharks. Its slope is then 0, and it usually stays dead.

  1. Choose "The loss does not move from 1.6" (it falls slowly to 1.23): the gradient lines of layers 1 to 3 are below 1e-6, far under layer 5 (near 0.02).
  2. Choose "The loss sticks at 1.23, gradients are 0": the gradient lines stop early (the norms fall to 0) and layers 3 and 4 show 100% dead units.
  3. Choose "The loss starts huge, then freezes": the first loss is 9.14. Then pick a cause under "Your diagnosis" and test it with the fixes.

Three runs end at loss 1.2: gradients below 1e-6 in early layers, gradients of 0 after a normal start, and gradients of 0 after a start at 9.1.

How it works

The answer to the guess is three or more, as the table of three runs shows. Take the first run of the table, the bad start, where the weights start as random numbers of typical size 0.005. Small weights give small output scores that differ little, so its output is nearly the same for all sharks. A network with one output for all sharks has its lowest loss, 1.23, when its probabilities equal the proportions of the species. The Go deeper part of the first section works out the sum.

runfirst lossfinal gradient normsfinal dead units, layers 1 to 4
bad start (weights of size 0.005)1.61below 1e-6 in layers 1 to 30%, 4%, 25%, 54%
dead units (learning rate 0.5)1.4804%, 42%, 100%, 100%
raw inputs (not standardised)9.14096%, 75%, 100%, 100%

Common belief. If the loss does not fall, the learning rate is wrong, so lower it.

Why it fails. The lab offers a lower rate for five of the six faults (the bad start gets a higher one). A lower rate fixes two of them (the run whose loss turns into NaN and the dead-unit run) and hides a third (raw inputs: the run trains, but the first loss is still 9.1). It leaves two as they were (labels that do not match their rows, exploding gradients).

Better account. Read the three numbers to find where the fault is, change one thing, then look again. Shuffled labels are the exception: these numbers look healthy, and the validation results show the fault (accuracy 32%, below the lazy model's 48%).

Quick quiz

Name two quick checks that separate the bad-start run from the dead-unit run, which both end at loss 1.23.

The gradient norm per layer: a bad start gives tiny norms (below 1e-6 in layers 1 to 3) after a normal first loss, and dead units give norms of 0. The dead-unit bars: 25% and 54% in layers 3 and 4 for the bad start, and 100% in both for the dead-unit run.

The shuffled-label run has healthy gradient norms and a falling training loss. What single number shows the fault?

The validation accuracy, 32%, which is below the lazy model's 48%. A network that fits labels that do not match their rows learns no rule that transfers to new sharks, and here its accuracy is below the lazy model's.

How to use the lab

Work through the six symptoms. For a symptom, look first at the loss and its first value. Then look at the gradient plot (a line is missing where the norm is 0), the update ratio and the dead-unit bars. Choose a diagnosis before you try a fix, then test it. A fix that works is evidence for a cause. A fix that makes no difference is evidence against that cause. A cause can be tested by changing one thing and looking again. The lab also has fixes that look good and are not. Adam rescues the badly initialised network, but the cause is still there. A lower rate rescues the raw-input run (74%) but the first loss is still 9.1.

The network has four hidden layers of 24 units and is trained on 480 made-up catch records with SGD and momentum 0.9 (the NaN run uses plain SGD). The regression run predicts weight in kg. A run has one seed, so differences of a few points in accuracy are noise. For the bad start the lab offers a higher rate instead, which makes it worse.

The bad-start run in detail

The badly initialised run starts at a loss of 1.61, which is right for five species, and its validation loss ends at 1.24 with an accuracy of 48.3%, the lazy model's. Its gradient norms are about \(5\times10^{-7}\) in layers 1 to 3, and the update ratio of layer 1 is \(4\times10^{-7}\). The code below shows what the network learned. The spread of its output scores across the sharks is 0.0000 for all five species. The last-layer bias equals the log of the class share plus about 2.1 to 2.2 for four species and 2.9 for the rarest. The softmax is unchanged when the same constant is added to all scores, so the biases alone give probabilities close to the species shares, with the rarest a little too high (45% spadenose, 33% milk, 12% bamboo, 9.5% hammerhead and 0.5% Ganges shark). The network has stored the base rates in its last bias, and its output no longer depends on its inputs. In this lab, a loss that stays at 1.23 is the loss of such a network.

The raw-input and dead-unit runs

The raw-input run has a different story behind the same end. Its first loss is 9.14, and its output scores have a spread of 22, against 0.8 for the standardised inputs. At a rate of 0.05 the first step changes layer 1 by 11% of its size (gradient norm 13.8, weight norm 6.4). That is about 50 times the 0.002 of the standardised run at the same rate. By the end, 96% of the units in layer 1 are dead. The dead-unit run has a third story. Its loss starts at 1.48, its rate is 0.5, and at the end all the units of layers 3 and 4 are dead.

In Python

import json, math, numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn

rec = json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"]
species = ["spadenose", "milk", "bamboo", "hammerhead", "ganges"]
cols = ["length_cm", "weight_kg", "girth_cm", "depth_m", "temp_c", "month"]
X = np.array([[r[c] for c in cols] for r in rec], dtype=np.float32)
y = torch.tensor([species.index(r["species"]) for r in rec])
p = np.random.RandomState(0).permutation(len(rec)); tr, va = p[:480], p[480:]       # 480 for training, 120 for validation
X_raw = torch.tensor(X)
X_std = torch.tensor((X - X[tr].mean(0)) / X[tr].std(0))

def network(spread=None, seed=0):                 # four hidden layers of 24 ReLU units
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(6, 24), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(24, 24), nn.ReLU(),
                        nn.Linear(24, 24), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(24, 24), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(24, 5))
    lins = [m for m in net if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)]
    for k, m in enumerate(lins):
        fan_in = m.weight.shape[1]
        std = spread or math.sqrt((1 if k == len(lins) - 1 else 2) / fan_in)    # He, or one fixed spread
        nn.init.normal_(m.weight, 0, std); nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
    return net

def first_look(name, net, X):
    """Numbers to read before the first update."""
    loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(X[tr]), y[tr])
    net.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(X[tr[:32]]), y[tr[:32]]).backward()
    g = [m.weight.grad.norm().item() for m in net if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)]
    print(f"{name:17s} start loss {loss.item():5.2f}  gradient norms", " ".join("%.0e" % v for v in g))

first_look("He, standardised", network(), X_std)
first_look("spread 0.005", network(spread=0.005), X_std)
first_look("He, raw inputs", network(), X_raw)

net = network(spread=0.005)                                   # now train the badly started network
opt = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.02, momentum=0.9)
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
for step in range(375):
    i = torch.tensor(tr)[torch.randint(0, 480, (32,), generator=g)]
    opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(X_std[i]), y[i]).backward(); opt.step()
with torch.no_grad():
    out = net(X_std[va])
    print("after 375 steps: validation loss %.2f, accuracy %.3f" % (nn.functional.cross_entropy(out, y[va]).item(), (out.argmax(1) == y[va]).float().mean().item()))
    print("spread of the scores across sharks:", out.std(0).numpy().round(4))
    print("last-layer bias minus log class share:", (net[-1].bias.numpy() - np.log(np.bincount(y[tr].numpy()) / 480)).round(2))

spread 0.005      start loss  1.61  gradient norms 4e-08 5e-08 5e-08 6e-08 5e-08
He, raw inputs    start loss  9.14  gradient norms 2e+01 3e+01 3e+01 5e+01 7e+01
after 375 steps: validation loss 1.24, accuracy 0.483
spread of the scores across sharks: [0. 0. 0. 0. 0.]
last-layer bias minus log class share: [2.17 2.08 2.22 2.09 2.94]

The first three lines are the numbers to read before the first update. A bad start shows in the starting loss (9.14), in the gradient norms (tiny, or in the tens) or in neither. The last three lines are the network after 375 steps of training.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Change one thing at a time. The lab lets you switch on two fixes together, and the result can hide which of them did the work. In the NaN run, clipping alone and a wider network alone both fail, but together they train.

More questions

In the NaN run, clipping at norm 1.0 stops the NaN. Why is that not a fix?

The steps are capped, but the learning rate is still far too high for this network. Many units die (100% of layer 4), the loss stays at 1.25 and the accuracy is the lazy model's. The cause, the rate, was not changed.

Gradient norms and the update-to-weight ratio

Guess first. In a five-layer network the gradient norm, the length of the loss slopes of a layer's weights, is 6e-7 in layer 1 and 2e-2 in layer 5. The loss is falling a little. Is the network fine, or is there a problem with the early layers?

In plain SGD (without momentum), one step changes the weights of a layer by \(\eta\lVert g\rVert\) in length, where \(\eta\) is the learning rate and \(\lVert g\rVert\) the gradient norm. Whether that is large depends on the size of the weights. So we divide by the weight norm \(\lVert\theta\rVert\), the length of the layer's weights as one vector, and get the update-to-weight ratio \(r = \eta\lVert g\rVert/\lVert\theta\rVert\). A common guideline is that a layer learns at a sensible speed when \(r\) is about \(10^{-3}\). A layer whose \(r\) is far below that value, while other layers are near it, hardly learns.

  1. With the sliders as they start (learning rate 0.020, gradient norm 1.0, weight norm 10) the diamond marks \(r = 2.0\)e-3, inside the teal band (about 3e-4 to 3e-3), the usual range.
  2. Drag the gradient norm down to 0.0010: \(r\) falls to 2.0e-6 and the verdict reads "far too small: the layer is barely learning".

At rate 0.02, gradient norm 1 and weight norm 10, one step changes the layer by 0.2% of its size, inside the usual range.

How it works

The answer to the guess is a problem. The guess uses gradient norms from the lab's run with a bad start, whose logged ratios are \(3.7\times10^{-7}\) in layer 1 and 0.005 in layer 5. So layer 5 changes more than 10,000 times faster relative to its size. The calculations below use \(\eta = 0.02\) and the plain formula. They give about half of the lab's logged ratios (0.0017 and \(1.9\times10^{-7}\) against 0.0032 and \(3.7\times10^{-7}\) in layer 1), probably because the lab uses momentum 0.9 and logs the largest value in an interval. A layer of \(n\) weights of size \(w\) has norm about \(\sqrt n\,w\). Here \(n = 6\times24 = 144\) (6 inputs, 24 units), so \(\sqrt{144}\times0.6 \approx 7\) and \(\sqrt{144}\times0.005 = 0.06\).

\(\eta = 0.02\)learning rate×\(\lVert g\rVert = 0.6\)layer 1 of a healthy run÷\(\lVert\theta\rVert = 7\)6 by 24 weights of size about 0.6=\(r = 0.0017\)0.2% per step|\(\eta = 0.02\)learning rate×\(\lVert g\rVert = 5.8\times10^{-7}\)layer 1 of the bad start÷\(\lVert\theta\rVert = 0.06\)weights of size 0.005=\(r = 1.9\times10^{-7}\)per step

Common belief. If the loss is falling, all layers are learning.

Why it fails. In the run with a bad start the loss falls from 1.61 to 1.23, but layers 1 to 3 hardly change: only the last layer learns.

Better account. Log the gradient norm and the ratio of all layers at intervals of 50 to 100 steps, and compare the layers with one another and with their own past. The value \(10^{-3}\) is a rough guide for plain SGD. Momentum 0.9 can make steps up to 10 times larger. With Adam the ratio is at most about \(\eta\) divided by the typical weight size, which it reaches at the first step.

Quick quiz

Rate 0.01, gradient norm 2, weight norm 40, plain SGD. What is the ratio, and is it in the usual range?

\(0.01\times2/40 = 5\times10^{-4}\). That is inside the usual band (about \(3\times10^{-4}\) to \(3\times10^{-3}\)), on its low side, a little below \(10^{-3}\).

Two layers have the same gradient norm, 0.5. With plain SGD and rate 0.01, their weight norms are 7 and 70. Which layer changes faster relative to its size, and by what factor?

The first. Its ratio is \(0.01\times0.5/7 = 7\times10^{-4}\), against \(7\times10^{-5}\) for the second: a factor of 10, the ratio of the weight norms.

The guess, with the lab's numbers

The numbers of the guess are from the badly initialised run of the lab. If all steps pointed the same way, layer 1 would need 1/(3.7e-7), about 2.7 million steps, to change by its own size, while layer 5, at 0.005, moves more than 10,000 times faster. In a healthy run of the same network the figure of the lab (which logs the largest value in an interval) shows gradient norms of the five layers between about 0.2 and 1.5, with a median near 0.7. The ratios have a median near 0.0035. The picture of the slopes sent back and multiplied layer by layer is the one of B4, and B6 shows how the starting scale decides it.

A rule of thumb, and the optimiser

The ratio is a rule of thumb from the CS231n notes, which suggest about \(10^{-3}\). A lower ratio can mean that the learning rate is too low, and a higher one that it is probably too high. The rule depends on the optimiser. For plain SGD the step is \(\eta\,g\), so the ratio is \(\eta\lVert g\rVert/\lVert\theta\rVert\). For Adam the step of a weight is about \(\eta\) whatever its slope (B5). The ratio then depends on \(\eta\) and the weight sizes, and you should look for a layer that is far from the others. In practice, plot the logged gradient norms and ratios on a log axis. A sudden change in one layer is a better clue than any absolute number.

Histograms over time

A histogram over time is the distribution of the gradients or activations of a layer, drawn at intervals during training. This chapter does not draw it. The lab shows the per-layer norms and the dead-unit bars instead, which are cheaper to log.

Symbols

\[ r \;=\; \frac{\lVert \Delta\theta\rVert}{\lVert\theta\rVert} \;=\; \frac{\eta\,\lVert g\rVert}{\lVert\theta\rVert} \quad\text{(plain SGD)} \]

  • \(r\) is the update-to-weight ratio of one layer. \(\Delta\theta\) is the change of the layer's weights in one step and \(\theta\) the weights themselves, with the norm taken over the whole layer.
  • \(\eta\) is the learning rate and \(g\) the gradient of the layer. With momentum \(\beta\) the steady step is up to \(1/(1-\beta)\) times larger, which is 10 times for \(\beta = 0.9\). The lab's logged values are 2 to 10 times the plain formula.

The two layers by the numbers

The worked example under "How it works" uses numbers from the lab. For the healthy layer the plain formula gives 0.0017 and the logged value is 0.0032, about 2 times higher. A likely reason is momentum, and the log also keeps the largest value in an interval. For the badly initialised layer the formula gives 1.9e-7 and the log shows 3.7e-7. The weight norm of the healthy layer is about 7 (6.9 for weights of size 0.58), and that of the bad layer is 0.06 for weights of size 0.005. What matters is the gap between the two layers, a factor of about 9,000 (0.0017 against 1.9e-7).

The ratio under Adam

At its first step Adam moves a weight with slope \(g\) by \(\eta\,g/(\lvert g\rvert + \epsilon)\), where \(\epsilon\) is 10\(^{-8}\). Later steps use running averages in place of \(g\), and no step is much larger than \(\eta\). When \(\lvert g\rvert\) is far above \(\epsilon\), all weights move by about \(\eta\) at the first step. A layer of \(n\) weights then moves by \(\eta\sqrt n\) and has a norm of \(\sqrt n\,\bar w\), so \(r \approx \eta/\bar w\). Here \(\bar w\) is the root mean square weight. For later steps this is a rough ceiling. With \(\eta = 0.01\) and the lab's healthy first layer (\(\bar w = 0.54\)) it gives 0.019. The lab's run with He initialisation and Adam logs 0.019 at step 1 and about 0.004 near the end, when the slopes of different batches disagree. The bad start breaks the condition. In the lab's Adam run from the bad start (rate 0.01) the first-layer slope at step 1 is about \(3.6\times10^{-9}\) per weight, below \(\epsilon\). The step is only 26% of \(\eta\), and the ratio is 0.53, near the 0.46 that was logged. At step 2 the logged ratio is 0.83. Plain SGD in the same start had a ratio of \(10^{-8}\). Adam rescues the run because its step does not shrink with the slope until the slope falls below \(\epsilon\).

g = 3.6×10−9slope per weight, layer 1→0.26g ÷ (g + 10−8)→0.032step of the layer: 0.01 × 0.26 × 12→0.53÷ 0.06, the weight norm

In Python

The code below logs the gradient norm and the update ratio of all five layers for 375 steps of SGD with momentum 0.9, in the healthy network and in the badly initialised one, and prints the medians. It continues the code of the lab section. The healthy network has medians near 0.4 to 0.5 for the gradient and 0.002 to 0.007 for the ratio. The bad start has \(5\times10^{-8}\) and \(2\times10^{-7}\) in layer 1, and \(7\times10^{-3}\) and \(5\times10^{-3}\) in layer 5. Only the last layer learns, which is the base-rate network above. These medians run over all 375 steps, so they are lower than the figure, which logs the largest value in an interval near the end of the run.

# continues the lab code above
def log_run(net, X, lr=0.02, steps=375):
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=0.9)
    lins = [m for m in net if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)]
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0); norms, ratios = [], []
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = torch.tensor(tr)[torch.randint(0, 480, (32,), generator=g)]
        before = [m.weight.detach().clone() for m in lins]
        opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(X[i]), y[i]).backward()
        norms.append([m.weight.grad.norm().item() for m in lins])
        opt.step()
        ratios.append([((m.weight.detach() - b).norm() / b.norm()).item() for m, b in zip(lins, before)])
    return np.array(norms), np.array(ratios)

for name, net in [("He", network()), ("spread 0.005", network(spread=0.005))]:
    n, r = log_run(net, X_std)
    print("%-12s median gradient norm" % name, " ".join("%.0e" % v for v in np.median(n, 0)))
    print("%-12s median update ratio " % name, " ".join("%.0e" % v for v in np.median(r, 0)))

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a layer's gradient is 0 for many steps, count its dead units before you touch the rate. A gradient that is small but not 0 points at the scale of the weights. A gradient of 0 points at dead units or a disconnected part of the graph.

More questions

Adam with \(\eta = 0.001\) trains a layer whose typical weight is 0.05. What ratio do you expect, and is it in the usual range?

\(r \approx \eta/\bar w = 0.001/0.05 = 0.02\) at most. That is up to 20 times the usual \(10^{-3}\), so the layer may move fast. Log the ratio to see, then lower the rate or check why the weights are so small.

Gradient clipping

Guess first. One batch of sharks gives a gradient (the vector of loss slopes for the weights) that is 20 times longer than usual. You rescale it to length 1 before the weight update. Does the update still point in the same direction?

An exploding gradient is so long that one step wrecks the weights. Clipping by norm limits it. If the length \(\lVert g\rVert\) of the whole gradient \(g\) (all layers together) is above a threshold \(c\), we multiply \(g\) by \(c/\lVert g\rVert\). This shortens \(g\) to length \(c\) and keeps its direction. Clipping by value instead cuts the components of \(g\) to the range \([-c, c]\) separately, and this can change the direction.

  1. The coral arrow is the gradient \(g = (1.9,\,0.9)\), and the dashed circle has radius \(c = 1\). The teal arrow, the clipped gradient, ends on the circle on the same line as \(g\), and the readout shows 25° before and after.
  2. Press "clip all components (changes it)": the circle becomes a square, and for \(g = (1.9,\,0.9)\) the direction turns from 25° to 42°.
  3. Drag the coral arrow, or move the slider "Threshold c". While the coral arrow is outside the circle, the teal arrow ends on the circle on the same line.

Clipping by norm shortens the arrow to the circle along the same line; clipping by value cuts it at the square and turns \(g = (1.9,\,0.9)\) from 25° to 42°.

How it works

Take \(g = (1.9,\,0.9)\) and \(c = 1\). The length is \(\lVert g\rVert = \sqrt{1.9^2 + 0.9^2} = \sqrt{4.42} = 2.10\), which is above \(c\), so we multiply both components by \(c/\lVert g\rVert = 1/2.10 = 0.476\). This gives \((0.90,\,0.43)\), with length 1 and the same direction, because both components are scaled alike. So the answer to the guess is yes for clipping by norm in plain SGD, where the update is a fixed multiple of the clipped gradient. Now take the lab's exploding run, which trains a network to predict a shark's weight in kg (the target), with the squared error, the square of the miss, as the loss. For a similar network at the start of training, the code in Go deeper gives the batch of the 32 heaviest sharks a gradient of length \(\lVert g\rVert = 95.5\). The factor at \(c = 1\) is then \(1/95.5 = 0.0105\). In the lab's exploding run the largest length is 284.

\(g = (1.9,\,0.9)\)length 2.10×\(\min(1,\, c/\lVert g\rVert)\)c = 1: min(1, 0.476)=(0.90, 0.43)length 1, same direction|\(\lVert g\rVert = 95.5\)the 32 heaviest sharks→\(\min(1,\, 1/95.5)\)c = 1=0.0105the factor
  1. The lines are the validation error of the exploding run. Without clipping (coral) it ends at 1.78 kg², and with clipping at norm 1.0 (teal) at 0.13 kg².
  2. Choose "update size ÷ weight size, layer 1". Without clipping the ratio reaches about 0.05 at times, 50 times the dashed line at 1e-3. With clipping it stays near or below that line.

Common belief. Clipping fixes exploding gradients.

Why it fails. It caps the length of a step and so treats the symptom. In the exploding run a likely cause is the target: the sharks' weights run from 0.02 to 59 kg. Predicting the log of the weight removes the heavy tail (a few very large values), and the loss then falls smoothly with no clipping at all.

Better account. Use clipping as a guard. Log the norm before clipping and choose \(c\) a little above the typical norm, so that only extreme batches are cut. If the clip is active on most steps (79% here at \(c = 1\); the threshold test is in Go deeper), look for another fault.

Quick quiz

The gradient is (3, 4) and \(c = 2\). Give the result of clipping by norm and by value.

The length is 5, so by norm the factor is 2/5 = 0.4 and the result is \((1.2,\,1.6)\), with length 2. By value both components are cut to 2, giving \((2,\,2)\), whose direction is 45 degrees against 53 degrees for the original.

What does the factor \(\min(1, c/\lVert g\rVert)\) do when the gradient is shorter than \(c\)?

It equals 1, so the gradient is unchanged. Clipping changes only the batches whose gradient is longer than \(c\).

Where clipping comes from

The idea comes from Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio (2013), who proposed it for recurrent networks, where exploding gradients are common. Exploding slopes are explained in the chapter on backpropagation.

About the exploding run

The target is the shark's weight in kg with squared error, and the heaviest sharks of the made-up table (up to 58.6 kg) produce gradients far above the normal batch. Both runs of the figure use the same network, data and seed, with one run per setting. With clipping at norm 1.0 the ratio of layer 1 stays between 0.0002 and 0.001 after the first steps.

Symbols

\[ g \;\leftarrow\; g\cdot\min\!\Big(1,\; \frac{c}{\lVert g\rVert}\Big) \qquad\quad \lVert g\rVert = \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_j g_j^{2}} \]

  • \(g\) is the vector of all weight slopes, in all layers together, and \(\lVert g\rVert\) its length. \(c\) is the threshold you choose.
  • If \(\lVert g\rVert \le c\) the factor is 1 and the gradient is unchanged. If \(\lVert g\rVert > c\) the factor \(c/\lVert g\rVert\) shrinks the length to \(c\) while all components are scaled alike, so the direction is kept. Clipping by value cuts the components apart and so can bend the direction.

In Python

import json, numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn

rec = json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"]
cols = ["length_cm", "girth_cm", "depth_m", "temp_c", "month"]
X = np.array([[r[c] for c in cols] for r in rec], dtype=np.float32)
X = torch.tensor((X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0))
w = torch.tensor([r["weight_kg"] for r in rec])            # the target, in kg

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(5, 24), nn.ReLU(),
                    nn.Linear(24, 24), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(24, 1))

def grad_norms(idx):
    net.zero_grad()
    loss = ((net(X[idx]).squeeze(1) - w[idx]) ** 2).mean()
    loss.backward()
    norms = [p.grad.norm().item() for p in net.parameters() if p.dim() == 2]
    return loss.item(), norms

batches = {"32 ordinary sharks": torch.arange(32),
           "the 32 heaviest": torch.argsort(w)[-32:]}
for name, idx in batches.items():
    loss, g = grad_norms(idx)
    total = np.sqrt(sum(v * v for v in g))
    print(f"{name:19s} loss {loss:7.2f}  layers {np.round(g, 1)}  total {total:.1f}")

before = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(net.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
after = torch.sqrt(sum((p.grad ** 2).sum() for p in net.parameters()))
print(f"clip_grad_norm_ returned {before:.2f}; norm after clipping {after:.2f}")
32 ordinary sharks  loss    5.70  layers [0.8 2.6 3. ]  total 4.1
the 32 heaviest     loss  346.83  layers [19.6 77.1 47. ]  total 92.4
clip_grad_norm_ returned 95.52; norm after clipping 1.00

The code prints one network at the start of training, on made-up records. The heaviest batch has a gradient about 23 times larger than the ordinary one (92.4 against 4.1), so with plain SGD one step on it would move the weights 23 times farther. The function returns the norm before clipping, 95.5 (it also counts the bias terms, hence a little above the 92.4 of the weight matrices), and the norm after is 1.00.

Where clipping misleads, and in practice

The lab's fix that treats the cause of the exploding run is to predict the log of the weight (as in A2). Its numbers are in log units, so compare the behaviour of the curves, not the values. A threshold that is too low acts like a smaller learning rate on all batches. In practice, log the norm before clipping and look at its distribution over a few hundred steps. Choose \(c\) a little above the typical norm so that only the extreme batches are cut. If the clip is active on most steps, the threshold is too low, the rate is too high, or the data has a problem to fix first. Values near 1 are a common starting point.

Choosing the threshold

The exploding run was repeated with six settings: no clipping and five thresholds (one seed, SGD with momentum 0.9, rate 0.003, validation error after 372 steps). With no clipping the error is 1.78. At \(c = 30\) it is 10.7 and at 10 it is 6.8, both worse. At 3 it is 0.88, at 1 it is 0.13 and at 0.3 it is 0.32. The unclipped gradient norms of this run have a median of 3.2, a 90th percentile of 28 and a maximum of 284. At \(c = 1\) the clip is active on 79% of the steps. By the rule of this section that points to another fault, and here a likely cause is the target: the weights run from 0.02 to 59 kg, and the log target is the better cure. One seed is a weak basis for a rule. Repeated for seeds 0 to 4, the median error is 4.1 with no clip, 1.2 at \(c = 30\), 0.74 at 10, 0.62 at 3, 0.09 at 1 and 0.40 at 0.3. In the median the high thresholds are then no worse than no clip. The runs at \(c = 30\) still range from 0.25 to 53. At \(c = 1\) all five errors (0.06 to 0.16) are below the best error of any other setting (0.19).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Clip after backward() and before step(). Clipping after the step has no effect, and clipping before the backward pass has no gradient to rescale.

More questions

Why does clipping not hide a learning rate that is too high?

It caps the size of one step, but a rate that is too high also causes oscillation and dead units in steps below the cap. In the lab's NaN run the clipped network still stays at the base-rate loss.

The threshold test shows clipping at \(c = 30\) ending worse than no clipping. What should you do before you conclude that high thresholds hurt?

Repeat the test with several seeds. The result is one run, and seed-to-seed spread is large (the reproducibility section). With seeds 0 to 4 the median error at \(c = 30\) is 1.2, against 4.1 with no clip. Also log how often the clip fires, because a threshold that never fires and one that fires on most steps are different faults.

A learning-rate range test

Guess first. You train for 200 steps while the learning rate rises from 0.00001 to 3. The loss falls, reaches a lowest point, then rises again. Where would you choose the rate for a long run: at the lowest point, well before it, or after it?

In a learning-rate range test the rate is multiplied by the same factor from one step to the next while we record the loss. We smooth the loss, which means averaging it over the last few steps so that batch noise does not hide the trend. The smoothed curve shows the rates at which the loss falls and the divergence point, where the loss rises above its starting value. Together they give a bracket of rates, a lowest and a highest rate to try, for a long run.

  1. On the left plot the navy curve is the smoothed loss: it is nearly flat below 0.0003, falls steeply from 0.003 to 0.03, is lowest near 0.07 and rises steeply above 0.4.
  2. Click the left plot, or use the slider, to show the run at one fixed rate. On the right plot, rates of 0.003 and 0.01 give the lowest validation losses, 0.65 and 0.68, and at 0.3 and above the validation loss stays at 1.2 to 1.3.

The smoothed loss is lowest near rate 0.07, yet the fixed-rate runs have their lowest validation losses at 0.003 and 0.01, well before that point.

How it works

Take the 200-step test of the figure. The rate goes from \(\eta_{\min} = 10^{-5}\) to \(\eta_{\max} = 3\) and is multiplied by the same factor, \((3/10^{-5})^{1/199} = 1.0654\), from one step to the next, a rise of 6.5% per step. The smoothed loss is lowest, at 0.71, at step 140, where the rate is \(10^{-5}\times1.0654^{140} = 0.071\). Because that loss was measured while the rate was still rising, a common rule takes a tenth of the rate, 0.007, as the first rate to try. If the loss is still falling at the highest rate, the test has not reached the divergence point, so extend the top rate.

\(\eta_t = 0.0057\)the rate at step \(t = 100\)=\(\eta_{\min} = 10^{-5}\)the first rate×\((\eta_{\max}/\eta_{\min})^{t/T}\)\(\eta_{\max} = 3\), \(T = 199\) steps from the first to the last rate

Common belief. The rate at the lowest smoothed loss is the best rate for a long run.

Why it fails. The test measures the loss while the rate is still rising, so the weights have had little time at that rate. In this lab a fixed-rate run at 0.1, near the lowest point, ends after 375 steps with a validation loss of 0.84, against 0.65 at 0.003. A usual reason is that a rate which is best for 200 steps can be too high to stay stable for thousands of steps, which the lab does not test.

Better account. Treat the steep part of the curve, 0.003 to 0.03, as the bracket, and try a rate near the middle of it first.

Quick quiz

The smoothed loss of a range test is lowest at rate 0.2. Which rate do you try first for a long run, and why not 0.2?

About a tenth of it, 0.02. The loss at 0.2 was measured while the rate was still rising. A rate that is best during a 200-step rise can be too high to stay stable for thousands of steps.

In a range test the loss is still falling at the highest rate. What does that tell you?

The test stopped too early. Extend the top rate until the loss rises, otherwise you know only the lower end of the good range.

Go deeper two rules, the ramp, Python, more questions about 4 min

Where the test comes from, and the fixed-rate runs

Smith (2017; first posted in 2015) described the test in the paper on cyclical learning rates, as a way to find the bounds of a good range. In the figure, the fixed-rate run at 0.3 ends at a loss of 1.23, the loss of a network that uses only the base rates.

About the figure

The ten fixed-rate runs use SGD with momentum 0.9 on the 480 made-up records, with one seed per run. The smoothed loss of the test is a running average of the batch loss, with weight 0.9 on the old value (see running averages).

Two ways to read the curve

The first rule takes a tenth of the rate at the lowest smoothed loss. That loss is 0.71 at a rate of 0.071, so the rule gives 0.007. The second rule takes the rate where the loss falls fastest per tenfold rise of the rate. The code below finds it near 0.023, where the smoothed loss falls by 1.2 per tenfold rise (the figure's own run puts it near 0.018, because its batch order differs). Compare both with the fixed-rate runs. The validation loss is 0.65 at 0.003, 0.68 at 0.01 and 0.77 at 0.03. The first rule gives a rate between the two best rates, 0.003 and 0.01. The second gives one between 0.01 and 0.03. Both are in the good band. Neither rate was run itself. The first lies between the two best runs. The second lies between the runs with losses 0.68 and 0.77. So the first looks safer, though another seed could change the order.

The ramp itself

The rate rises by 6.5% per step, so it takes 73 steps to go from \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-3}\), more than a third of the run, and the smoothed loss falls only from 1.49 to 1.38 there. At step 100 it is 1.19, and the lowest point, 0.71, comes at step 140, so most of the fall (0.48 of 0.78) happens between steps 100 and 140.

In Python

# continues the lab code above
def range_test(lo=1e-5, hi=3.0, steps=200, batch=32):
    net = network()
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=lo, momentum=0.9)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0); order = torch.randperm(480, generator=g); pos = 0
    rates, smooth, ema = [], [], None
    for t in range(steps):
        lr = lo * (hi / lo) ** (t / (steps - 1))                  # the rate rises by the same factor from one step to the next
        for group in opt.param_groups: group["lr"] = lr
        if pos + batch > 480: order = torch.randperm(480, generator=g); pos = 0
        i = torch.tensor(tr)[order[pos:pos + batch]]; pos += batch
        opt.zero_grad(); loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(X_std[i]), y[i]); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        ema = loss.item() if ema is None else 0.9 * ema + 0.1 * loss.item()       # smoothed loss
        rates.append(lr); smooth.append(ema)
    return np.array(rates), np.array(smooth)

rates, smooth = range_test()
low = smooth.argmin()
slope = np.gradient(smooth, np.log10(rates))                      # change of the smoothed loss per tenfold rise of the rate
steep = slope[:low + 1].argmin()
print("lowest smoothed loss %.3f at rate %.3f" % (smooth[low], rates[low]))
print("rule 1, a tenth of the lowest point: %.4f" % (rates[low] / 10))
print("rule 2, steepest fall: rate %.4f (loss falls %.2f per tenfold rise)" % (rates[steep], -slope[steep]))
lowest smoothed loss 0.707 at rate 0.071
rule 1, a tenth of the lowest point: 0.0071
rule 2, steepest fall: rate 0.0228 (loss falls 1.16 per tenfold rise)

Symbols

\[ \eta_t \;=\; \eta_{\min}\Big(\frac{\eta_{\max}}{\eta_{\min}}\Big)^{t/T} \]

  • \(\eta_t\) is the rate at step \(t\), \(T\) the number of steps of the test (199 intervals for 200 steps), and \(\eta_{\min}\), \(\eta_{\max}\) the first and last rates. Equal steps on a log scale make the curve readable on a log axis.

Where the test misleads, and in practice

The best rate for a long run is often lower than the rate that is fastest in the first 200 steps. It changes with the batch size, with warm-up and with the schedule (B5). The loss curve of the test is noisy with small batches, hence the smoothing, and the lowest point moves from seed to seed. In practice, run the test once for a new model or data set, starting from the initial weights. Stop when the loss is more than about four times its best value. Treat the result as a bracket of rates to try, and try a rate near the middle of the bracket first.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the loss stays flat for the whole range test, even at a rate of 1, check two things. The optimiser must be updating the weights (the update ratio is not 0), and the loss must be connected to the model's output.

More questions

With the ramp of the worked example, at which step is the rate 0.07, and why does the lowest loss come after the steep fall?

The rate is \(10^{-5}\times1.0654^{t}\), so \(t = \ln(7000)/\ln(1.0654) = 140\). The loss falls while the rate is useful and levels off when the steps become too long. The smoothed value lags the rate by a few steps, so its lowest point comes a little after the best rate.

Learning curves, bias and variance

Guess first. A species classifier gets 25% of the training sharks wrong (its training error) and 29% of the validation sharks wrong (its validation error). Would 10 times more training sharks help it greatly, slightly or not at all?

A learning curve plots the training error and the validation error (the error on sharks kept out of training) against the number of training sharks. Two gaps on the plot help us choose the next step. Avoidable bias is the training error above a target, the best error we hope for (here a made-up goal of 0.20). A better model, better inputs or longer training can reduce it. Variance is the gap between the validation error and the training error, and more data, a smaller model or a penalty on large weights can reduce it.

  1. Choose "too simple: length only", with the slider at 384 sharks. The training error (navy dot) is 0.25 and the validation error (coral dot) is 0.29, both above the dashed target at 0.20. Drag the slider to 48 sharks: the validation error is 0.29 too.
  2. Choose "too flexible: 128 + 128 units" (two layers of 128 units). The training error is 0.00 at all sizes, and the validation error falls from 0.40 at 12 sharks to 0.30 at 384 and is still falling.

At 384 sharks the too simple model has errors 0.25 and 0.29 on flat curves, the too flexible model 0.00 and 0.30 on a falling validation curve.

How it works

Take the too simple model at 384 sharks. Its avoidable bias is 0.05 and its variance is 0.04 (equation below). More data mainly shrinks the gap between the validation and training errors. Here the validation curve is already flat: from 48 to 384 sharks, eight times more data, it moved from 0.291 to 0.294. So, as far as this curve shows, the answer to the guess is not at all, and closing the whole gap would lower the validation error by only 0.04. This model uses the length only. The other two models (about right, and too flexible) use all six measurements of the made-up catch records (length, weight, girth, depth, temperature and month) and reach lower training errors.

avoidable bias0.05=training error0.25−target0.20|variance0.04=validation error0.29−training error0.25

Common belief. More data lowers the validation error.

Why it fails. More data can shrink the gap between the curves, but the validation error usually stays above the training error. The training error of the too simple model stays between 0.23 and 0.26 from 12 to 384 sharks.

Better account. Plot the curves before collecting more data. A training error above the target needs a bigger model, better inputs or longer training. A large gap with a validation curve that is still falling needs more data, a smaller model or a penalty on large weights.

Quick quiz

A model has training error 0.02, validation error 0.22 and target 0.10. What are its avoidable bias and variance, and what would you try first?

The avoidable bias is 0 (0.02 is below the target) and the variance is \(0.22 - 0.02 = 0.20\). Try more data, a smaller model or a penalty on large weights.

A model has training error 0.30, validation error 0.32 and target 0.10, and the last doubling of the data lowered the validation error by 0.001. What do you try?

The avoidable bias is 0.20 and the variance is 0.02, so the fit of the model itself limits it and more data cannot help. Try a bigger model, better inputs or longer training.

Go deeper Ng's argument, the other models, Python, limits about 5 min

The guess, with Ng's argument

This is Ng's argument in Machine Learning Yearning (chapters 20 to 32). The training error shows bias, and the difference between validation and training error shows variance. If the training error is already above the desired level, more data cannot repair that, and with more data the training error usually rises a little. In the flexible model the training error is about 0 for all sizes while the validation error falls from 0.40 to 0.30 and has not stopped. Here more data helps, and so does a penalty or a smaller network.

Ng's decomposition

Ng's decomposition takes the best achievable error (his "optimal error rate") into account: total error is optimal error plus avoidable bias plus variance. Avoidable bias is training error minus optimal error, and variance is validation error minus training error. In the figure the target of 0.20 replaces the optimal error. For the simple model at 384 sharks both terms are modest (0.05 and 0.04). It uses the length only, while the other two models use all six measurements of the table (length, weight, girth, depth, temperature and month). For the flexible model the avoidable bias is 0 (training error is below the target) and the variance is 0.30. For high avoidable bias, try a bigger model, new inputs or longer training. For high variance, try more data, a penalty (B7), augmentation (extra training examples made by changing existing ones) or a smaller model.

About the figure

The curves are means of 10 networks on the made-up records, and the validation set has 120 sharks. At 384 sharks the middle model has a training error of 0.18 and a validation error of 0.26. The target of 0.20 is a made-up working goal, close to the error of the trees of A5 and A6.

The other two models by the numbers

The simple model improves from 0.358 to 0.291 as the data grows from 12 to 48 sharks, then stays between 0.291 and 0.294 up to 384. Eight times more sharks changed the validation error by 0.003, and its training error is already 0.25. This is the case of the guess: more data does not help, and a better model or new inputs are the options to try. For the medium model, the validation error falls by 0.027 from 96 to 192 sharks (0.304 to 0.277) and by 0.019 from 192 to 384 (to 0.258). The gains shrink as the data doubles. If the next doubling gave about 0.013, the error would be near 0.245, still above the target of 0.20. This is an extrapolation and no measurement, and it suggests that more data alone will be slow.

In Python

import numpy as np

# training and validation error at 12, 24, 48, 96, 192 and 384 sharks (mean of 10 networks, made-up records)
curves = {
    "simple":   ([.233, .250, .258, .261, .264, .249], [.358, .308, .291, .294, .293, .294]),
    "medium":   ([.000, .021, .083, .133, .173, .178], [.387, .328, .332, .304, .277, .258]),
    "flexible": ([.000, .000, .000, .000, .000, .002], [.396, .356, .358, .345, .336, .298]),
}
target = 0.20                                    # a made-up working goal
for name, (train, val) in curves.items():
    train, val = np.array(train), np.array(val)
    bias = max(train[-1] - target, 0)            # avoidable bias: training error above the target
    variance = val[-1] - train[-1]               # gap between validation and training error
    gain = val[-2] - val[-1]                     # what the last doubling of the data bought
    advice = "more sharks will not help" if gain < 0.005 else "more sharks help"
    print("%-8s bias %.3f  variance %.3f  gain from 192 to 384 sharks %+.3f  -> %s" % (name, bias, variance, gain, advice))
simple   bias 0.049  variance 0.045  gain from 192 to 384 sharks -0.001  -> more sharks will not help
medium   bias 0.000  variance 0.080  gain from 192 to 384 sharks +0.019  -> more sharks help
flexible bias 0.000  variance 0.296  gain from 192 to 384 sharks +0.038  -> more sharks help

The last number of a line is the one to watch. It is the gain from the most recent doubling of the data, and when it falls under half a point the curve has flattened.

Where the curves mislead, and in practice

The optimal error is unknown and is often not 0. Some sharks of different species in the made-up table may look alike in all six measurements, and then even the best model makes errors. Curves from few runs are noisy (Ng recommends averaging or plotting more sizes), and a validation set of 120 sharks gives an interval of several points (A4). The diagnosis also assumes the training and validation sets come from the same source. If they do not, a gap can come from the shift and not from variance. In practice, plot the curve before collecting more data, because collecting is expensive and the curve is cheap.

More questions

Why does the training error rise as you add data for the flexible model?

With 12 sharks a large network can memorise all of them. With 384 it fits almost all of them, so training error rises slightly (0.002 at 384). Ng notes that training error usually rises as the training set grows.

Reproducibility: changing one thing and knowing it mattered

Guess first. You train the same network twice with two learning rates, 0.02 and 0.03, and the second run has a validation accuracy 1 point higher than the first. Is 0.03 better?

A seed is the number that starts a random generator, so the same seed gives the same random numbers (see random numbers in Python). The seed sets the initial weights and the order of the batches. So a different seed usually gives a different accuracy for the same settings, and the spread (standard deviation) of the accuracy across seeds is the noise of an experiment. A difference between two single runs that is smaller than this spread is not evidence. So change one thing, run several seeds, and compare the two settings seed by seed, which is a paired comparison.

  1. Navy dots are 20 runs at rate 0.02 and coral diamonds are 20 runs at rate 0.03, and the black bars are the means, 72% and 71%. In the paired view (the first button) a grey line joins the two runs of one seed.
  2. Press "show the runs unpaired": the 40 dots lose their lines and the two clouds overlap. The readout gives the paired difference, −0.5 ± 1.4 points.

With 20 seeds, rate 0.02 averages 72% and rate 0.03 averages 71%, and the paired difference is −0.5 ± 1.4 points, so these runs do not show a difference.

How it works

Subtract the two accuracies seed by seed. The 20 differences have a mean of \(-0.5\) points and a standard deviation of \(s = 3.18\). The standard error \(s/\sqrt n\) is the typical error of a mean of \(n\) values, here \(s/\sqrt{20} = 0.71\). The 95% interval is the mean \(\pm\) 1.96 standard errors (the confidence interval), here \(-0.5 \pm 1.4\). It contains 0, so these 20 seeds do not show that 0.03 is better, and the answer to the guess is not yet. A single pair of runs is weaker evidence. The spread across seeds is 4.4 points at rate 0.02 and 3.8 at rate 0.03, so two runs can differ by 1 point or by 8 points by chance. Pairing helps because the two runs of one seed share the initial weights and the batch order, so luck that helps both runs cancels in the difference. This is why the differences vary less (s = 3.18 points) than the difference of two unrelated runs would (5.8 points, from \(\sqrt{4.4^2 + 3.8^2}\)).

interval−0.5 ± 1.4 points=\(\bar d = -0.5\)mean difference of the 20 pairs±1.96for 95%×\(s/\sqrt{n} = 0.71\)\(s = 3.18\) points, \(n = 20\) seeds

Common belief. A fixed seed makes a comparison trustworthy.

Why it fails. A fixed seed can make one run repeatable on the same machine and software. A different seed changes the accuracy by points, so a comparison with one seed may show only the luck of that seed. Even a fixed seed does not guarantee the same numbers on all computers. Some operations on a GPU (the chip that does most of the work in training) can give slightly different results on repeated runs.

Better account. Change one setting at a time, log the seed, the settings and the code version, run several seeds, compare them in pairs and report the spread.

Quick quiz

Two settings differ by 2 points, the seed spread is 4 points and there are 3 seeds per setting. Do you accept the difference?

No. With 3 seeds the standard error of a mean is about \(4/\sqrt3 = 2.3\) points, so a 2-point difference is within the noise. Run more seeds, or pair them.

Why is a paired comparison tighter than a comparison of two means?

A pair shares the seed, so luck that helps both runs, such as a good initial draw, cancels in the difference. Here the standard error is 0.71 when the runs are paired and 1.29 when they are treated as unrelated.

Go deeper the guess, repeated runs, seeds needed, Python about 5 min

The guess in detail

A second example, from the pipeline of the next section: with the same data split, six different network seeds give validation accuracies of 75.0%, 80.0%, 75.8%, 77.5%, 75.0% and 75.0%. With the same network seed and six different splits they range from 78.3% to 85.8%.

About the figure

The network, the made-up data and the settings are the same in all 40 runs. Only the seed, which sets the initial weights and the batch order, changes. The comparison of the two rates is the paired test of the probability chapter.

Repeating a run

seed 0, run 1: validation accuracy 0.750
seed 0, run 2: validation accuracy 0.750
same split, network seeds 1 to 6: 0.750 0.800 0.758 0.775 0.750 0.750
same network seed, splits 1 to 6: 0.783 0.858 0.792 0.817 0.808 0.800

These four lines come from the repaired pipeline of the next section, run 14 times with the numbers in np.random.default_rng(...) and torch.manual_seed(...) changed. Two identical runs give identical numbers, because all sources of randomness have a seed: torch.manual_seed for the weights and dropout, a seeded NumPy generator for the shuffle and the split. The first two lines of the output show this.

The paired interval, and how many seeds you need

The code below takes the 20 accuracies of both rates and subtracts them seed by seed, as in the worked example. Treating the two groups as unrelated gives a standard error of 1.29, because that keeps the seed-to-seed spread which pairing removes. The same 20 seeds give an interval 1.8 times narrower when they are paired. The standard deviation of the differences, 3.2 points, is smaller than that of two unrelated runs combined, \(\sqrt{4.4^2 + 3.8^2} = 5.8\) points.

How many seeds you need. To see a gain of \(\delta\) points you need an interval narrower than \(\delta\). That means \(1.96\,s/\sqrt n \le \delta\), so \(n \ge (1.96\,s/\delta)^2\). With \(s = 3.2\) that is at least 5 seeds for a 3-point gain and 10 for a 2-point gain. These counts are floors. With so few seeds the multiplier 1.96 should be a t-value (2.8 for 5 seeds), which raises them to 7 and 13. A gain equal to the half-width of the interval is also found only about half the time.

import numpy as np

# validation accuracy in %, 20 seeds, at rate 0.02 and rate 0.03 (made-up records; the same seed in the same position)
a = np.array([74.2, 69.2, 65.8, 68.3, 78.3, 76.7, 72.5, 75.0, 67.5, 67.5, 65.8, 65.8, 75.8, 72.5, 72.5, 75.8, 79.2, 75.8, 70.8, 68.3])
b = np.array([71.7, 69.2, 67.5, 72.5, 75.8, 78.3, 70.8, 73.3, 69.2, 71.7, 65.0, 66.7, 78.3, 74.2, 69.2, 72.5, 75.0, 68.3, 66.7, 71.7])
d = b - a                                                # one difference per seed
se = d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d))                     # standard error of the mean difference
print("means %.1f and %.1f; spread of one setting %.1f points" % (a.mean(), b.mean(), a.std(ddof=1)))
print("paired difference %.1f, sd %.1f, standard error %.2f, interval +-%.1f" % (d.mean(), d.std(ddof=1), se, 1.96 * se))
print("unpaired standard error of the difference: %.2f" % np.sqrt(a.var(ddof=1) / 20 + b.var(ddof=1) / 20))
for gain in (3, 2):                                      # seeds needed so that the interval is narrower than the gain
    print("to see a %d-point gain with paired sd %.1f you need at least %d seeds" % (gain, d.std(ddof=1), np.ceil((1.96 * d.std(ddof=1) / gain) ** 2)))
means 71.9 and 71.4; spread of one setting 4.4 points
paired difference -0.5, sd 3.2, standard error 0.71, interval +-1.4
unpaired standard error of the difference: 1.29
to see a 3-point gain with paired sd 3.2 you need at least 5 seeds
to see a 2-point gain with paired sd 3.2 you need at least 10 seeds

Where the comparison misleads, and in practice

Logging means writing down the settings, the seed and the scores of a run, so that you can repeat or compare it. A seed does not guarantee the same numbers on another machine. Some GPU operations are not deterministic, data loaders that use several workers can change the order, and library versions change the numbers. PyTorch has an option to ask for deterministic algorithms, at a cost in speed. Twenty seeds are also many for a large model. In practice: log the seed, the settings and the code version of a run. Change one setting at a time. Use at least 3 to 5 seeds for any comparison whose effect is a few points. Report the spread and not the best run. Selecting the best of many seeds and reporting it is a form of peeking at the validation set (A4).

More questions

Two settings differ by 3 points on average over 5 paired seeds, and the differences have a standard deviation of 3.2. Give the 95% interval. Is the gain shown?

The standard error is \(3.2/\sqrt5 = 1.43\). With the multiplier 1.96 the interval is \(3 \pm 2.8\), from 0.2 to 5.8. For 5 seeds the right multiplier is the t-value 2.78, which gives \(3 \pm 4.0\), from \(-1.0\) to 7.0. It contains 0, so the gain is suggested and not shown. Run more seeds.

Test one component at a time

Guess first. A pipeline, all the code from the data to the evaluation (in the Go deeper part below), trains a small network on the made-up catch records. It has four bugs and runs without errors. Its validation accuracy is 0.45, the lazy model's on its own 120 validation sharks (the lazy model always says the commonest species, and the lab's split gives 48%). You have eight small tests. What is the smallest number of them that point at all four bugs: two, three or four?

A failing training run shows that something is wrong, and a test of one component shows which. Components are the parts of the pipeline: the data, the model, the loss, the update step and the evaluation. A unit test checks one component against an output you know in advance, and a suspect is a bug that a failing test points at.

  1. Tick Test 1, "look at one shark you know": the row for Tag 5519 should be a hammerhead, and it says spadenose, so the labels do not belong to their rows.
  2. Tick Test 2, the starting loss: it reads 1.613 against \(\ln 5 = 1.609\) and passes, but all four bugs leave it near \(\ln 5\).
  3. Keep ticking until the status line reads "Suspects found: 4 of 4": Tests 1, 4 and 6 are enough.

All four suspects found. The fixes, in the order of the code, are as follows. Use one permutation for both arrays instead of two shuffles. Drop nn.Softmax, because CrossEntropyLoss applies its own. Call opt.zero_grad() before loss.backward(). Call model.eval() for the validation pass and model.train() afterwards. The repaired pipeline scores 0.750, and its overfit-one-batch test reaches a loss of 0.069 where the broken one stalled at 1.47.

One more detail is not a bug of the four. The standardising step uses the mean and spread of all 600 rows, validation rows included. That is a small leak of the kind A4 describes. It does not matter here, but a careful pipeline computes them on the training rows only.

Six of the eight tests fail and five point at a bug, while the two that pass miss all four bugs.

How it works

The four bugs are labels shuffled apart from their rows and a softmax inside the model that the loss applies again. CrossEntropyLoss applies a softmax itself, so the model should output raw scores. The other two bugs are a missing zero_grad (which clears the slopes of the previous step) and dropout (units switched off at random in training) left on during validation. Test 5 calls backward three times with no zero_grad in between, and the gradient norm of layer 1 grows as 0.1075, 0.2151 and 0.3226, where it should repeat. Test 8 prints the network's output for two rows; the outputs are probabilities that sum to 1, so the model already ends in a softmax. Test 4, overfit one small batch (train on 16 sharks until the loss is near 0), flags the extra softmax and the missing zero_grad together. So three tests, 1 (labels), 4 and 6 (evaluation mode), flag all four bugs, and Tests 1, 5, 6 and 8 point at one bug apiece.

four bugsaccuracy 0.450→shuffle fixed0.55→softmax removed0.058→zero_grad added0.767→evaluation mode0.750

Common belief. If the starting loss matches \(\ln K\) and the code runs without errors, the pipeline is correct.

Why it fails. The starting loss checks only the model and the loss at initialisation. All four bugs leave it near \(\ln 5\), and none raises an error.

Better account. Trust a pipeline only after its components have passed their own checks. Fix one bug at a time and test again, because a fix can uncover a bug that it was hiding. Here a likely case is the missing zero_grad: once the extra softmax no longer hides it, the gradients can grow without limit.

Quick quiz

Which test points at the label bug, and what does it read?

Test 1. It reads the row of a shark you know, Tag 5519, which must be a hammerhead, and finds the label spadenose.

Fixing the shuffle raises the accuracy from 0.450 to 0.55, but removing the extra softmax next lowers it to 0.058. What is a likely reason?

The fix uncovered another bug that was hiding behind it. A likely reason is that the missing zero_grad then lets the gradients grow without limit.

Go deeper the code, the guess, fixes, single bugs about 4 min

The pipeline

import json, numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn

rec = json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"]    # the made-up records
species = ["spadenose", "milk", "bamboo", "hammerhead", "ganges"]
cols = ["length_cm", "weight_kg", "girth_cm", "depth_m", "temp_c", "month"]
X = np.array([[r[c] for c in cols] for r in rec], dtype=np.float32)
y = np.array([species.index(r["species"]) for r in rec])

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
rng.shuffle(X); rng.shuffle(y)                    # mix up the rows
mu, sd = X.mean(0), X.std(0)
X = torch.tensor((X - mu) / sd); y = torch.tensor(y)   # standardise
Xtr, ytr, Xva, yva = X[:480], y[:480], X[480:], y[480:]

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(6, 24), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.3),
                      nn.Linear(24, 24), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(24, 5),
                      nn.Softmax(dim=1))
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05, momentum=0.9)

for epoch in range(30):
    for i in range(0, 480, 32):
        loss = loss_fn(model(Xtr[i:i+32]), ytr[i:i+32])
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    acc = (model(Xva).argmax(1) == yva).float().mean().item()
print(f"validation accuracy {acc:.3f}")
validation accuracy 0.450

The outputs of the tests are from running this code. The accuracy of the pipeline is 0.450 with the four bugs and 0.750 when they are fixed, on 120 validation sharks.

The guess in detail

The tests were chosen so that a test looks at one component. The data test reads the input and its label. The starting-loss test reads the model and the loss together. The overfit test reads the whole loop on a tiny batch. The gradient test isolates backward and zero_grad, the mode test isolates dropout, and the output print isolates the last layer. Tick them in any order. The overfit test also flags the double softmax and the missing zero_grad but cannot say which is which, so the data test (labels), the gradient test (zero_grad), the evaluation-mode test (dropout) and the output print (double softmax) are the four that separate the bugs. The lazy-baseline test shows that the model does no better than a guess, and not why. That is the usual value of a baseline: it tells you whether to keep looking.

Fixing the bugs one at a time

Fix the bugs one at a time, and test again after a fix (the accuracies are in the second layer). A likely reason for the drop to 0.058 is that the missing zero_grad now lets the gradients grow without limit. A fix can lower the accuracy before it raises it when it uncovers a bug that was hiding behind another. This is the practical reason for the one-component-at-a-time rule: with four changes at once you would not know which one helped.

One bug at a time

A second experiment puts one bug at a time back into the repaired pipeline. The validation accuracy is 0.450 with only the two separate shuffles, which is the lazy model's, so that bug alone leaves the network at the lazy model's accuracy. With only the missing zero_grad it is 0.433. With only the double softmax it is 0.775, and with only the dropout left on during validation it is 0.767, against 0.750 for the repaired pipeline. The last two stay inside the range of the six network seeds of the reproducibility section (75.0% to 80.0%), so an accuracy check alone would not find them. The tests do, because a test reads one component. A bug that leaves the accuracy alone on this data can matter elsewhere. The double softmax squeezes the scores into the range 0 to 1, which flattens the loss, and dropout during validation adds noise to all the numbers you compare. Starting from the broken pipeline, fixing a single bug raises the accuracy only for the shuffle (0.55) in these runs.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Write a test once as a short function and keep it with the code. The overfit-one-batch test and the check of one known shark take a minute to run, and here they flag three of the four bugs.

More questions

The softmax bug did not change the starting loss. Why?

The outputs after the first softmax are close to 0.2, and a second softmax of numbers near 0.2 is still close to uniform. The loss starts near \(\ln 5\) either way.

The double softmax alone leaves the accuracy at 0.775, above the repaired pipeline. Why is it still worth fixing?

It squeezes the scores into the range 0 to 1, so the loss is flat and the slopes are small. With five classes the second softmax gives the true class at most \(e/(e+4) = 0.40\), so the loss cannot fall below 0.90. Training is slower and the printed probabilities are not what the loss treats as scores. Here the data is easy enough to hide this, and a harder problem would not.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory (a) What starting loss do you expect for a 4-class problem with random weights? (b) A model predicts the class shares 0.5, 0.3, 0.15 and 0.05 for all sharks, and the labels have those shares. What is its loss? (c) Is a network with a starting loss of 1.1 on the 5-species problem good news?

    Hint

    For (b) the loss is the entropy \(-\sum p \ln p\). For (c) compare 1.1 with \(\ln 5\) and ask what it would mean.

  2. theory The gradient is \((3, 4)\) and the threshold is \(c = 2\). Compute the result of clipping by norm and clipping by value, and the angle of both from the first axis. Then say which one keeps the direction and why.

  3. theory A layer has weight norm 20 and gradient norm 0.5, and the rate is \(\eta = 0.01\) with plain SGD. (a) What is the update-to-weight ratio? (b) How many steps does it take to change the layer by its own norm if the gradient stayed constant in size? (c) If the optimiser uses momentum 0.9 and the gradient has a constant direction, how does the steady ratio change?

    Hint

    With momentum \(\beta\) and a constant gradient the velocity grows to \(1/(1-\beta)\) times the gradient.

  4. theory A model has training error 0.12 and validation error 0.30. The best known error for the task is 0.10. Compute the avoidable bias and the variance. Then say which of these changes you would try first: a deeper network, 5 times more training data, a weight penalty, longer training.

Practice

  1. practice Take the buggy pipeline of the last section. Fix the four bugs one at a time, and after a fix print the validation accuracy. Does the score rise after all four fixes? Explain any step where it falls.

    Hint

    The scores are 0.45, 0.55, 0.06, 0.77 and 0.75 in the order shuffle, softmax, zero_grad, mode. The 0.06 comes from a fix that uncovers another bug.

  2. practice Run a learning-rate range test on the repaired pipeline: 200 steps with the rate rising from 1e-5 to 3, smoothed loss against the rate on a log axis. Choose a rate with the ten-times rule and train for 30 epochs. Compare with the rate 0.05 of the pipeline.

  3. practice Add logging to the repaired pipeline: after an epoch print the gradient norm and the update-to-weight ratio of the three linear layers. Find the layer with the smallest ratio and say whether the pattern is healthy.

Think deeper

  1. open A teammate reports that a new SharkCam classifier "works" because it scores 75% on validation. List what you would check before you agree, in order, and say what a result of a check would make you conclude.

  2. open Design a one-page training dashboard for SharkCam with six plots or numbers. Say what the items show, which fault it would reveal and what you would do when it looks wrong.

  3. open You want to know whether a change improves validation accuracy by 1 point on a model whose seed-to-seed spread is 3 points. How many paired seeds do you need, what could go wrong with the pairing, and what would make you stop early?

Come back later

(B4, B8) A twelve-layer sigmoid network has a gradient of size 7.5e-8 reaching layer 1 and about 0.2 at layer 12. Which number of the lab shows this, and what does the update ratio of layer 1 look like?

The gradient norm per layer, which falls by the factor 0.227 per layer of B4 across 12 layers. The update ratio of layer 1 is tiny, like the 3.7e-7 of the badly initialised lab run, so layer 1 barely learns. The cure is in B6: a better initial scale, normalisation or shortcuts.

(A4, B8) A learning curve shows validation error flat at 0.29 while training error falls from 0.25 to 0.0. What do you conclude about the model and what do you try?

The model is memorising: variance is large. Try more data, a weight penalty or augmentation (B7), or a smaller network, and use early stopping with the validation curve.

(B5, B7, B8) After fine-tuning on a new water the validation score is good. Which two checks of this chapter and B7 should you also run?

Score the old water's held-out set again, to catch forgetting (B7). Compare with a lazy baseline and a few seeds, so that a good score is not noise or chance (B8).

Sources and further reading

  1. Karpathy, A. (2019). A recipe for training neural networks. Blog post, 25 April 2019. The order of the routine: become one with the data, the training skeleton with dumb baselines, overfit, regularise, tune.
  2. Ng, A. (2018). Machine Learning Yearning, draft chapters 13 and 14 (first system, error analysis), 20 to 25 (bias and variance), 28 to 32 (learning curves). Free from deeplearning.ai.
  3. Stanford CS231n, Neural networks, part 3: learning and evaluation. Sanity checks (the starting loss, a tiny training set), the update-to-weight ratio of about 1e-3 and the reading of loss curves.
  4. Pascanu, R., Mikolov, T., and Bengio, Y. (2013). On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks. ICML 2013 (PMLR 28); arXiv:1211.5063, first posted in 2012. Gradient norm clipping.
  5. Smith, L. N. (2017). Cyclical learning rates for training neural networks. WACV 2017; arXiv:1506.01186, first posted in 2015. The learning-rate range test: raise the rate for a few epochs and watch the loss.
  6. Zhang, C., Bengio, S., Hardt, M., Recht, B., and Vinyals, O. (2017). Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization. ICLR 2017; arXiv:1611.03530. Networks can fit random labels.
  7. Reference for the data: the made-up catch records of the SharkCam table (see the notes of B7), 600 records, 480 for training and 120 for validation in the lab.

The lab's 48 runs, the range test, the learning curves and the pipeline outputs are from PyTorch runs with fixed seeds on the made-up records. A lab run is one seed and shows the mechanism, not a measure of how often it occurs.
